stops.note: a wooden beam; architects still call post-and-beam building 'trabeated'
'archi-', chief, plus 'trave', beam; Sebastiano Serlio's architecture books of the 1530s and 1540s spread such terms across Europe
French builders took it up with Italian Renaissance design
arrived as John Shute's 'First and Chief Groundes of Architecture' (1563) introduced the classical orders to English readers

current_meaning: the beam resting on top of classical columns; the moulding around a door or window frame
